title: Pure Land, closed
hook: a vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light

segments.voice: Yesterday, many views of the land: a real place in the west, a mind made pure, or both, with the name shared by all. Your line was more than one answer. Where did you let two answers stand? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

A vow. A name. A sunset. A land of light. If the Pure Land fit on a postcard, those four would be the picture. A monk long ago makes vows so large they need a whole world to hold them. A buddha's name becomes something anyone can say, a farmer, a queen in prison, a clog-maker at his bench. The sun goes down in the west like a drum hung in the sky. And beyond it, a land where even the birds teach. Today we close this part of the path, and look at it whole. Today: Pure Land.
screen: `A VOW. A NAME.` → `A SUNSET. A LAND OF LIGHT.` → `PURE LAND.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. We began with Sukhavati, the land of bliss, and the monk Dharmakara, who in the Larger Sukhavati-vyuha makes his great vows. At their heart is the primal vow: that anyone who calls his name with trust will be born in his land. Dharmakara becomes Amitabha, the Buddha of infinite light and infinite life. Second, the land and the seeing. The Smaller sutra described the jeweled trees and the birds that teach. Then Queen Vaidehi, locked away by her own son, asked for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha taught her to see it: the setting sun, then water, ice and crystal ground. Third, the name. The nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo. Tanluan and Shandao in China shaped the practice. In Japan, Shinran spoke of other power, tariki, and of shinjin, true entrusting, with the name said in gratitude. Rennyo carried it to farmers through simple letters. In China and Vietnam, people sit and call the name together. At the deathbed, the name is said with the dying. And the myokonin, like Saichi the clog-maker, lived it with quiet joy. Fourth, the land today. Temples far from Asia, some called churches. Teachers who say the land is also a mind made pure here. And more than one answer about what the land is, held side by side. What runs through all of it is light. Amitabha's name means infinite light, and the tradition holds that this light leaves no one out. Tomorrow a new part begins: the traditions of Tibet.
screen: `THE VOW: DHARMAKARA BECOMES AMITABHA.` · `THE LAND: TREES, BIRDS, A SETTING SUN.` · `THE NAME: SAID IN TRUST AND THANKS.` · `THE LAND TODAY: HERE, THERE, BOTH.` · then, large: `INFINITE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit comfortably and let your hands rest. If you say the nembutsu, you can say it now, once or a few times, Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo, slowly, and then stop. If you don't, simply hold the words infinite light in mind for one breath. Then rest. Don't do anything more. Let the light, whatever it means to you, do the rest of the sitting. The bell holds the time.
Pure Land. The tradition of Amitabha Buddha: a vow, a name said with trust, a land of light in the west and, for some teachers, a mind made pure here. Today's word.
Your line: infinite light. Today, at sunset or whenever the light changes, stop for one breath and look west. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan and Namo Amituofo in China, in temple services, at home, with the dying, and in gratitude, trusting the vow of a Buddha of infinite light.

fork.setup: you're Queen Vaidehi, locked away by your own son. the Buddha comes to you. what do you ask for?
fork.reveal: she asks for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha teaches her to see it, starting with the setting sun.

original.note: Sanskrit: Amitabha, infinite light. in Japan, Amida; in China, Amituo.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pure Land is a heaven for good people.
what it means: a land made by a buddha's vow, reached by calling his name with trust, and for some teachers a mind made pure here.
what a scholar hears: one vow, read many ways, from Shandao's land in the west to Shinran's birth settled in this life.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavati-vyuha (Dharmakara's vows; the primal vow)
Amitayur-dhyana Sutra (Vaidehi; the setting sun, water and ice)

notes: Block close for Block G · Pure Land (days 1255–1275): names each day's word from the index. Several of these days were not on disk when this was written, so the recap follows the index lines.
The count of Dharmakara's vows (forty-eight, the day-1256 carry) was left out on purpose, since versions of the Larger Sukhavati-vyuha number them differently.
'The tradition holds that this light leaves no one out' paraphrases Pure Land teaching on Amitabha's light; confirm.
Sanskrit अमिताभ and the gloss 'infinite light': confirm.
